findings.claim: The Kurma Purana (1:6, 1:9, 1:26) is one of the scriptural sources for this concept.
findings.truth: The specification cites only Kurma Purana 1.6 and 1.9 for the trimurti. The third reference, 1:26, is not in the specification and cannot be verified. Drop it so students cite what the paper expects.
findings.evidence: spec Component 3 Option 2 Hinduism, Hindu Gods/deities: 'Nature and role of the trimurti (Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva and their consorts); Kurma Purana 1.6, 1.9'

findings.claim: Mark scheme for 'Give two names used for God in Hinduism' accepts 'Atman (as divine within)'.
findings.truth: Atman is the individual soul, not a name for God. The lesson itself defines atman as the individual self, distinct from Brahman. A student who wrote 'atman' would not gain the mark, and the accept-list contradicts the lesson.
findings.evidence: spec Component 3 Hinduism, The Eternal Self: 'Atman; trapped in matter, distinct from body and mind'; lesson 1 glossary definition of atman

findings.claim: Bhagavad Gita 2:17 states that the soul is indestructible: the body may be slain, but the soul that pervades the body cannot be destroyed.
findings.truth: 2:17 does teach that what pervades the body is indestructible, so the core claim is right and the specification cites 2:17 for atman. The 'the body may be slain' wording belongs to 2:20 ('it is not slain when the body is slain'). Not worth an edit, but worth knowing if the verse is ever quoted verbatim.
findings.evidence: Bhagavad Gita 2.17 and 2.20; spec cites 'Bhagavad Gita 2.12, 2.17' for atman

findings.claim: For the 15-mark evaluate question, remember to include a non-religious perspective alongside religious ones.
findings.truth: On the world-faith paper a non-religious view is allowed but is not required. The specification says only that awareness of humanism and atheism 'may be applied throughout the assessment'. The advice is safe but overstated; it is not wrong enough to edit.
findings.evidence: spec Component 3 Route A preamble; AO2 footnote: 'non-religious beliefs as appropriate to the subject content requirements'

findings.claim: Mundane (Head-Shaving Ceremony) - named as the Hindu head-shaving rite in the content, in the takeaways and as a knowledge-check option.
findings.truth: The rite is the Mundan (Sanskrit chudakarana). 'Mundane' is an English word meaning ordinary and is a transliteration error. The unit teaches the wrong Sanskrit term three times, including as a multiple-choice option.
findings.evidence: standard transliteration of the samskara; the same error repeats in conclusion_html and knowledge_checks[3].options[0]

findings.claim: Examiners reward the 'why' as well as the 'what'.
findings.truth: An invented claim about what examiners do. Replace with a neutral statement about where the marks come from.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims or mark-scheme voice

findings.claim: Two of the six practice questions test the samskaras: a 5-mark 'Describe the features and significance of the Hindu sacred thread ceremony (Upanayana)' and a 15-mark 'For Hindus, the most important rite of passage is cremation, not the sacred thread ceremony.'
findings.truth: The naming rite, the head-shaving rite and Upanayana appear nowhere in this specification. The world-faith practices are: daily and congregational puja, mandirs in Britain compared with India, outdoor shrines, havan, arati, darshan, bhajan/kirtan, japa, Diwali, Holi, Raksha Bandhan, pilgrimage to the Ganges at Varanasi, and social concern (Vrindaban environmental projects, goshallas, ISKCON Food for Life). Hindu marriage and Hindu funerals are examinable, but in the Route A themes on relationships and on life and death, not on this paper. Options: (a) leave the samskara content and its two questions as general world-faith background; or (b) keep the samskara content but swap the two questions for spec-anchored ones - Raksha Bandhan, mandirs in Britain compared with India, or ISKCON Food for Life and cow protection, none of which the unit covers. Option (b) needs two new mark schemes, so it is authoring work, not a surgical edit.
findings.evidence: spec Component 3 Option 2 Hinduism, Practices table (places of worship, worship/meditation, festivals, sacred sites, social concern); Hindu marriage at Theme 1 Issues of Relationships; Hindu funerals at Theme 2 Issues of Life and Death
findings.ruling: Leave: question re-setting is a build item (relabel queue).

findings.claim: For Shaktas (devotees of the goddess), Diwali is associated with the goddess Lakshmi ... and, in the key fact box, 'Diwali celebrates Rama and Sita's return (Vaishnavas) or honours Lakshmi (Shaktas).'
findings.truth: Lakshmi worship at Diwali is broad Hindu practice, strongest in northern and western India, and Lakshmi is Vishnu's wife - so it is a Vaishnava association, not a Shakta one. Shakta Hindus in eastern India (Bengal, Odisha, Assam) worship Kali on Diwali night. The lesson sets up a false contrast that a student would repeat.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Diwali: 'Many Hindus associate the festival with Goddess Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth and prosperity, and wife of Vishnu'; 'Hindus of eastern India associate the festival with the Goddess Kali'

findings.claim: examiners are looking for both knowledge of content and understanding of significance.
findings.truth: Another invented claim about examiner behaviour. Replace with a neutral statement about where the marks come from.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims or mark-scheme voice

findings.claim: All 18 practice mark schemes across the three lessons use the ladder Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging.
findings.truth: The house ladder is Top band / Upper-mid band / Mid band / Lower-mid band / Low band. This is a whole-unit relabel and belongs to the band-ladder queue, not to this fact-check.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md, banned strings and house band vocabulary

summary: Doctrine, scripture citations and all 15 knowledge-check answer keys are sound; the Bhagavad Gita, Chandogya and Katha references match the specification. Four fixes: the head-shaving rite is called 'Mundane' three times instead of Mundan, Diwali's Lakshmi association is wrongly assigned to Shaktas, atman is listed as an acceptable name for God, and two exam tips invent examiner behaviour. One adjudication: lesson 2 gives two of its six practice questions to samskaras, which this component does not examine.
